resources.string: Its history will be deleted too.
When you don’t know yet what you want, or want too much at once.
Lenses for any goal: clear wording, real motivation, a plan for obstacles.
The engine of a goal: how it is broken down and what you do each day. One per goal.
Find out how a goal could fail, before it does.
A goal, 8 pillars and 64 actions on one sheet

A 9×9 chart. Your goal sits in the centre, eight pillars surround it, and each pillar gets eight concrete actions: 64 in all. The whole road fits on one page, and the grid pushes you past the obvious. Ohtani’s chart had “luck” and “being liked” next to pitch speed.

Write the goal in the centre.
Name eight pillars: what has to be true to get there.
Give every pillar eight concrete actions.
Make some of them habits, take others on as one-off steps.
Light a star when an action has become part of you.
The Harada Method by Japanese coach Takashi Harada. Made famous by Shohei Ohtani, who filled one in at 16 with the goal of being the first draft pick of eight teams.
An inspiring objective and the numbers that prove it
An objective that excites you, plus three to five key results that are numbers. It runs for a quarter and is scored from 0 to 1. For an ambitious objective, 0.7 already counts as success.

Write the objective: in words, not numbers.
Add 3–5 key results, each with a start and a target.
List initiatives: what you’ll do to move the numbers.
Check in weekly: update the numbers and your confidence.
Score the quarter at the end.
Andy Grove at Intel in the 1970s. John Doerr brought it to Google in 1999, and from there it spread everywhere.
A year squeezed into 12 weeks, scored every week

Treat 12 weeks as a whole year. The deadline is always close, so there’s no time to put things off. Each week you score the share of planned tactics you actually did. 85% is excellent: execution, not results, is what you control.

Pick what you’ll achieve in 12 weeks.
Break it into weekly tactics.
Do them and tick them off every day.
Score every week, aiming for 85%.
Week 13 is for looking back and resting.
From the book “The 12 Week Year” by Brian Moran and Michael Lennington.
One key goal, the actions that drive it, a scoreboard

One wildly important goal with a lag measure: from X to Y by when. And one or two lead measures: actions you fully control that move the result. A simple scoreboard tells you every week whether you’re winning.

Choose one wildly important goal: from X to Y by a date.
Pick 1–2 lead measures that predict the result and are up to you.
Keep the scoreboard: are you winning this week?
Every week: look back, then commit to next week.
“The 4 Disciplines of Execution” by Chris McChesney, Sean Covey and Jim Huling, from FranklinCovey.
A little more every day, and it compounds
Start small and add a little every day. One percent a day feels like nothing, but it compounds: after 70 days you’re at double. Works for anything you can count: push-ups, pages, minutes, words.

Choose what to grow and an easy starting number.
Set the daily step: 1% or your own.
Every day, do today’s number and log it.
Watch the curve climb.
Kaizen is the Japanese practice of continuous improvement. James Clear’s “Atomic Habits” made the idea of getting 1% better every day popular.
An experiment, not a goal: try it for 30 days
Not a goal but an experiment: “I will do X for 30 days.” There’s no result to hit. You keep the pact and watch what happens. At the end you decide: persist, pause or pivot.

Phrase the pact: I will … for … days.
Tick every day you keep it.
Note what you notice along the way.
At the end, decide: persist, pause or pivot.
From “Tiny Experiments” by neuroscientist Anne-Laure Le Cunff. PACT stands for purposeful, actionable, continuous, trackable.
Start at the finish line and walk back to today

Start from the finish and walk backwards: what has to be done a month before? And before that? Keep going until you reach a step you can take this week. You end up with a dated plan that lands exactly on your goal.

Write the goal and its date.
Ask: what has to be done just before that?
Keep stepping back until you reach today.
Give each step a date.
Climb the ladder one rung at a time.
Backcasting, used in strategy and long-term planning since the 1970s.
A goal, a few checkpoints and habits, nothing more
A goal with a few milestones, and habits if you need them. For when a full method would be too much.
Name the goal and, if you like, a number to reach.\nAdd milestones along the way.\nAdd habits that move you forward.
Turn a wish into a clear, checkable goal

Five questions that turn a vague wish into a goal: is it specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound? A goal that passes all five is hard to misunderstand, even for you a month from now.

Specific: what exactly?
Measurable: how will you know you’re there?
Achievable: is it realistic with what you have?
Relevant: why this, why now?
Time-bound: by when?
George T. Doran, in a 1981 management article.
Wish, outcome, obstacle, plan: dreaming with a safety net

Positive thinking alone can make you less likely to act. WOOP adds the honest part: name the obstacle inside you and prepare an if-then plan for it. It’s one of the best-researched techniques for following through.

Wish: what do you want?
Outcome: picture the best result, vividly.
Obstacle: what inside you could get in the way?
Plan: if the obstacle shows up, then I will…
Psychologist Gabriele Oettingen, from two decades of research on mental contrasting and implementation intentions.
The coaching conversation you can have alone. Instead of jumping straight to a plan, look honestly at where you are and list options before choosing one.

Goal: what do you want?
Reality: where are you now? What have you tried?
Options: what could you do? List many.
Will: what will you do, and when?
Coaches Graham Alexander and John Whitmore, in the 1980s.
Dig down to the reason that will keep you going
Ask “why does this matter?” five times. Each answer goes deeper, and the last one is your real motivation. Read it on the days you want to give up.

Write why the goal matters.
Ask “and why does that matter?”
Repeat five times.
Keep the deepest answer close.
Sakichi Toyoda at Toyota, as a way to find the root cause of problems.
Imagine it failed, then make sure it won’t
Imagine it’s the deadline and the goal has failed. Why? Telling the story of failure in advance brings up risks that optimism hides. For every risk you write how to prevent it.

Imagine the deadline has passed and it didn’t work out.
Write down every reason why.
For each one, decide how to prevent it.
Keep the plans close and check them in reviews.
Psychologist Gary Klein, in Harvard Business Review, 2007.
See which areas of life need you most
Rate eight areas of life from 1 to 10. The wheel shows at a glance which areas are running low, and a goal there will change the most. Repeat every few months and compare.

Rate every area from 1 to 10, honestly.
Look for the dents in the wheel.
Pick one area to work on.
Check again in a few months.
Usually credited to Paul J. Meyer, founder of the Success Motivation Institute, in the 1960s.
Three different versions of your next five years

Sketch three different versions of your next five years: the life you’re on, the life if that path disappeared, and the life if money and other people’s opinions didn’t matter. Rate each one. Goals often appear by themselves.

Life 1: the path you’re already on.
Life 2: if that path vanished tomorrow.
Life 3: if money and opinions didn’t matter.
Rate each: resources, how much you like it, confidence, coherence.
Turn what pulls you into a goal.
Bill Burnett and Dave Evans, “Designing Your Life”, a Stanford course and book.
Write 25 goals, keep 5, avoid the other 20
Write down 25 things you want. Choose the five that matter most. The other 20 are not a backup list. They’re the “avoid at all costs” list, because they quietly steal time from the five.

Write 25 goals.
Choose the five most important.
The rest go on the avoid list.
Turn the five into goals.
Attributed to Warren Buffett through a story told by his pilot. Buffett said it isn’t his, but the idea works anyway.
Put a price on your dreams and they become a plan
List your dreams in three columns: having, being, doing. Put a price on each, one-off or monthly. Add them up into a target monthly income, and “someday” turns into a number you can plan for.

List what you’d like to have, to be and to do.
Price each dream: once, or per month.
See your target monthly income.
Turn the dream you can reach first into a goal.
